title: Deployment Strategies & Zero-Downtime Rollouts
summary: The Kubernetes-native mechanics — probes, rollout controls, PodDisruptionBudgets — that turn a deployment strategy from theory into a safe rollout.

slides.subTitle: maxSurge and maxUnavailable
slides.markdown:
A Deployment's default rolling update replaces old Pods with new ones gradually, governed by two knobs. **maxSurge** caps how many *extra* Pods beyond the desired count can exist during the rollout (capacity headroom). **maxUnavailable** caps how many Pods can be *missing* from the desired count at once (how much capacity you're willing to lose).

Defaults are 25% each. Set `maxUnavailable: 0` for a service that can't drop capacity at all — it forces every replacement Pod to be ready before an old one is removed, at the cost of needing surge capacity.

slides.subTitle: Readiness vs liveness vs startup
slides.markdown:
Three probes, three different questions.

| Probe | Question it answers | Failure action |
|---|---|---|
| Readiness | Can this Pod take traffic right now? | Removed from Service endpoints, not restarted |
| Liveness | Is this Pod stuck/deadlocked? | Container is restarted |
| Startup | Has slow-starting app finished booting? | Delays liveness/readiness checks until it passes |

A rolling update's safety hinges entirely on **readiness** — it's the signal that gates when a new Pod is allowed to receive traffic and an old one can be removed.

slides.subTitle: Missing readiness probe
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "the container starting is the same as being ready to serve traffic."

**Why it breaks:** with no readiness probe, Kubernetes marks a Pod ready the instant its container starts — even mid-cache-load or before its database connection exists. During a rollout, the Service sends live traffic to that not-actually-ready Pod, producing real errors.

**The correct model:** define a readiness probe checking what actually matters (a `/healthz` that returns 200 only once dependencies connect) — the most common cause of "the rollout looked clean but users saw errors."

Blue-green on Kubernetes isn't a built-in primitive — it's a pattern: run two full Deployments (`app-blue`, `app-green`), each fully scaled, and cut over by changing the Service's label **selector** from one to the other. The switch is instant and the old version stays fully running, so rollback is just flipping the selector back.

The cost is running double capacity during the cutover window — you're paying for two complete environments, however briefly, in exchange for an instant, all-or-nothing switch.

A basic canary needs no special tooling: run a second Deployment (`app-canary`) with a small replica count behind the **same** Service selector as the stable Deployment — Kubernetes load-balances across both, so the canary naturally gets roughly its share of traffic proportional to its replica count.

This is coarse (you can't easily do "5% of traffic" without matching replica ratios) — a service mesh gives fine-grained, percentage-based traffic splitting independent of replica counts, which is why mesh-driven canaries (Area's `api-gateway-mesh` group) exist for finer control.

Rolling updates are **voluntary disruptions** you control — but node drains for maintenance or a Cluster Autoscaler scale-down are voluntary too, and can otherwise take down more of a service than you'd like at once. A **PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)** sets a floor: "at least 2 of these 3 replicas must stay available," and voluntary disruptions are blocked from violating it.

A PDB has no effect on **involuntary** disruptions — a node crashing outright isn't stopped by a PDB, since there's no orderly eviction to block.

`kubectl rollout undo` works because Deployments keep a **revision history** of past ReplicaSets. Rolling back re-triggers the exact same rolling-update mechanism, just aimed at the previous ReplicaSet's Pod spec instead of a new one — it's not a special reverse operation, it's a forward rollout to an older target.

That's also why revision history has a limit (`revisionHistoryLimit`, default 10) — old ReplicaSets are kept scaled to zero purely so a rollback target still exists, and pruning them trims how far back you can undo.

slides.subTitle: Readiness probes catching a bad rollout
slides.markdown:
A new version fails to connect to its database on startup. With a real readiness probe checking that connection, the new Pods never turn Ready — the rollout stalls with old Pods still serving all traffic, and `kubectl rollout status` hangs instead of completing. Users see nothing.

Without that probe, the broken Pods would've been marked ready immediately, taken their share of traffic, and served errors until someone noticed and manually rolled back — the exact failure mode a readiness probe is built to prevent structurally, not through faster human reaction.
